c.tagline: Bolivia's whitewashed constitutional capital, where colonial grandeur meets dinosaur tracks.

taxi.fareNote: Taxis charge a flat per-trip rate (a few bolivianos within the center); agree it before departing. Shared 'trufi' taxis run fixed routes. Ride apps have limited coverage.

emergency.note: 110 reaches the police and 118 the ambulance service in Bolivia; 119 is the fire brigade. Response times can be slow outside the center.

avoid.reason: Watch for pickpockets in the Mercado Central and around the bus terminal, and take a taxi rather than walking to the terminal or cemetery area late at night.

hood_desc: The whitewashed UNESCO colonial core around Plaza 25 de Mayo, home to the Cathedral, Casa de la Libertad, universities, museums, cafes and most hotels; the ideal walkable base for first-timers.

A tranquil hillside neighborhood just southeast of the center around the Recoleta convent and its arched mirador, with some of Sucre's prettiest colonial houses and sweeping city views; peaceful and scenic.

The traditional artisan and market barrio on the slope west of the historic centre, built around the 17th-century Templo de San Roque and the busy Calle Loa and Junin streets; an unpolished, workaday quarter of cheap hostels and comedores about a 10-minute walk from Plaza 25 de Mayo.
lodging: El Jardin De Su Merced B&B

water.note: Drink bottled or purified water; avoid ice from unknown sources.

transit.hours: City micros generally run from around 6:00 AM to 10:00 PM; after that taxis and shared trufis are the main option.
transit.note: Sucre has no metro or rail. Public transport is a network of micros (small city buses) and shared trufi taxis on fixed routes, backed by regular taxis. The compact historic center is best explored on foot.
transit.pay: Fares are paid in cash to the driver on board (roughly Bs 2 per micro ride); there is no transit card. Carry small notes and coins.

bus: Intercity buses from the Terminal de Buses to Potosí, La Paz, Cochabamba and Santa Cruz

transit.m: Taxi to the city center (40-45 min)
Shared minibus / trufi from the airport toward the center (fills as it departs)

tip.r: Tipping is not deeply ingrained; 5-10% at tourist-oriented restaurants for good service is appreciated but not expected, and rounding up is fine elsewhere.

landmarks: Casa de la Libertad
The hallowed hall where Bolivia's declaration of independence was signed in 1825, now the country's most important historical museum on the main plaza.
Plaza 25 de Mayo
Sucre's palm-shaded colonial heart, ringed by gleaming whitewashed arcades, the cathedral and government buildings that earned the city UNESCO status.
Parque Cretácico and Cal Orck'o
A near-vertical limestone wall bearing over 5,000 real dinosaur footprints, the world's largest collection, viewed from a fun cretaceous-themed park.
Convento de la Recoleta and Mirador
A 1601 Franciscan monastery on a hillside plaza whose arcaded viewpoint frames the finest panorama of Sucre's white rooftops.
Convento de San Felipe Neri
A neoclassical convent whose rooftop terraces and bell towers offer dreamlike sunset views across the White City's domes and courtyards.
Catedral Metropolitana de Sucre
The city's 16th-century cathedral blends Renaissance and baroque styles and guards the jewel-encrusted Virgin of Guadalupe, Bolivia's most treasured icon.
Museo de Arte Indígena ASUR
An outstanding textile museum showcasing the intricate weavings of the Jalq'a and Tarabuco peoples, with weavers often demonstrating their craft live.
Castillo de La Glorieta
A fantastical pink palace mixing Gothic, Moorish and baroque towers, built by Bolivia's only 'prince and princess' in the 1890s.
Cementerio General de Sucre
An unexpectedly beautiful cemetery of marble mausoleums, cypress avenues and sculpted angels, long treasured by locals as a peaceful park.
Tarabuco Sunday Market
A vibrant highland market town an hour from Sucre where Yampara communities in distinctive dress trade legendary hand-woven textiles.

train.note: Sucre has a railway station and a line towards Potosi and Rio Mulatos, but no scheduled passenger trains use it - the track carries freight and the occasional special only. The nearest passenger services are Empresa Ferroviaria Andina's Expreso del Sur and Wara Wara del Sur (https://www.fca.com.bo/) on the Oruro - Uyuni - Tupiza - Villazon line, which means a bus to Uyuni or Oruro first. Bolivia has no through international passenger trains either: the southern line stops at Villazon on the Argentine frontier and the eastern line at Puerto Quijarro on the Brazilian one, and you cross both borders on foot.

bus.note: No coach runs across a border directly from Sucre - for Argentina you change at Villazon or Yacuiba, for Chile at Uyuni or La Paz, and for Brazil at Santa Cruz. The bus terminal is about 2 km from the centre, reached by micros 3 and A or a cheap taxi, with a small terminal fee payable at an office before boarding. Fares and times run roughly BOB10-35 and 3 hours to Potosi, BOB45-180 and 12 hours to La Paz, BOB35-110 and 14 hours to Santa Cruz, and BOB30-100 to Cochabamba; Trans Copacabana M.E.M., El Dorado and Boliviana offer the better semi-cama seats. Tickets are usually sold only on the day of departure, so go to the terminal before midday.

ferry.note: Sucre is a landlocked highland city at 2,800 m with no lake or navigable river, so no passenger boat services exist; Bolivia's only significant passenger boats are the Lake Titicaca crossings far to the northwest.

full.name: Potosí
